Judgment

The plaintiff has filed this suit as against the defendant seeking the relief of permanent injunction to restrain the defendant and its agents from interfering with the peaceful possession and enjoyment of the plaintiff over the suit schedule property.

2. Brief facts of the plaint averments are as under:-
O.S. No.26291/2020
The plaintiff is the absolute owner in possession of suit schedule property.
He acquired the same by virtue of registered sale deed dated 21.09.2020.
Due to over site some errors have crept in the sale deed and hence the vendor executed registered rectification deed on 12.10.2020.
The vendor of the plaintiff was absolute owner of 21 guntas in Sy.No.160 and out of that portion of the property ie.,
suit schedule property was given to the plaintiff through sale deed through his power of attorney holder.
3. It is the further case of the plaintiff that he paid up to date tax to the suit property, the khatha is also stands in his name.
The plaintiff has constructed house in the suit schedule property.
When things stood so the defendant came to suit schedule property without any prior notice on 03.11.2020 and warned the plaintiff that he will demolish the house in the schedule property.
The plaintiff complained the matter before the officers of the defendant.

It is the further case of the plaintiff that his vendor was in possession of suit schedule property for more than 70 years with knowledge and against to the interest of defendants and hence the defendants have lost claim for possession and thereby his vendors perfected the title of suit schedule property through adverse possession.
The defendant on 04.01.2020 directed the plaintiff to vacate the suit schedule property and has given 3 days time without issuing any prior notice and stated that the land has been acquired by BDA.
When the plaintiff went to police station to give complaint police refused to take his complaint and directed him to approach court.

The defendant contended that the suit is not maintainable, there is no cause of action to the suit, the defendant ie., BDA acquired the land in Sy.No.160 measuring 3 acres 5 guntas vide preliminary notification No.BDA/ALAl/S/11/78-79 dated 27.06.1978 and final notification No.HUD/567/MNX84 dated 09.01.1985 for formation of 'Hennur Bellary Road, 1 st stage'.

The defendant can demolish the unauthorized construction in accordance with law and in due process of law.
On the above grounds the defendant prays to dismiss the suit with exemplary costs.

sentences.text: It is necessary to note that the suit schedule property in the case on hand is property bearing khatha No.458/160, site No.209, formed in portion of assessment (Sy.)No.160, previously situated at Kacharakanahalli Village, now comes under BBMP.
The plaintiff also averred that the suit schedule property is O.S. No.26291/2020 portion of property in Sy.No.160 which was measuring 21 guntas.
According to plaintiff it is the said portion which is carved out of Sy.No.160 is given to him under registered sale deed dated 21.09.2020 by his vendor.

His vendor was the absolute owner of the suit schedule property and he was in possession of said property for more than 70 years and thereby his vendor perfected the title of the suit schedule property by way of adverse possession.
16. Hence from the plaint averments it is clear that the plaintiff is claiming title in respect of suit schedule property on the basis of registered sale deed dated 21.09.2020 marked as Ex.P4.

The plaintiff has also relied upon documents like khatha certificate issued by the BBMP, house and vacant sites register extract, rectification deed and GPA.
17.
The plaintiff has filed this suit on 07.11.2020.

According to plaintiff he is absolute owner of suit schedule property and since the date of sale deed ie., O.S. No.26291/2020 21.09.2020 he is in peaceful possession and enjoyment of the suit schedule property.

The documents relied on by the plaintiff ie., khatha certificate is issued on 26.03.2022, the house and vacant sites register is pertains to the period of 2022-23, the tax paid receipt Ex.P3 is also pertains to the period of 2022-23.

None of the documents produced by the plaintiff are pertains to the date of filing of this suit on the contrary they pertains to the period 2022 that means they are subsequent to the filing of the suit.
18. This is a suit for bare injunction and in a suit for bare injunction the title of the property is immaterial.
The plaintiff need not prove title of the property.
However in the case on hand as discussed supra the plaintiff has specifically pleaded and claiming title and ownership under the registered sale deed dated 21.09.2020.
According to plaintiff he acquired the suit schedule property from one C.Nagaraj, by his GPA holder K.S.Satish Kumar.

When the plaintiff has O.S.
No.26291/2020 specifically asserted that he acquired the suit schedule property by virtue of registered sale deed dated 21.09.2020 the plaintiff has to establish the said fact.
The plaintiff has to establish flow of title in respect of suit schedule property to his vendor C.Nagaraj.

The plaintiff also asserted that his vendor was in possession of suit schedule property since 70 years within the knowledge of defendant and thereby his vendor perfected title to suit schedule property through adverse possession.
Therefore the title of the suit schedule property is required to be considered incidentally.

19. On perusal of the sale deed-Ex.P4 it is stated in page No.2 that the vendor of the land bearing assessment No.160 of Kacharakanahalli out of which schedule A property was formed is the ancestral property of the vendor having acquired the same by him by way of succession and inheritance.

However, in the plaint the plaintiff pleaded that his vendor was O.S. No.26291/2020 absolute owner of Suit schedule property and his vendor perfected title to suit schedule property by way of adverse possession.
However no piece of evidence to show the possession of his vendor or title of vendor in respect of suit schedule property is produced by the plaintiff.

24. The defendant in his written statement has categorically denied the title and so also the possession of the plaintiff over the suit schedule property and contended that Sy.No.160 measuring 3 acres 5 guntas was already acquired by way of passing preliminary notification and final notification.

When there is a denial of the title of the plaintiff in respect of suit schedule property the plaintiff has to establish the flow of title and he has to file suit for declaration of title and not suit for bare injunction.

sentences.text: We may however clarify that a prayer for declaration will be necessary only if the denial of title by the defendant or challenge to plaintiff's title raises a cloud on the title of plaintiff to the property.
A cloud is said to raise over a person's title, when some apparent defect in his title to a property, or when some prima facie right of a third party over it, is made out or shown.
An action for declaration, is the remedy to remove the cloud on the title to the property.

On the other hand, where the plaintiff has clear title supported by documents, if a trespasser without any claim to title or an interloper without any apparent title, merely denies the plaintiff's title, it does not amount to raising a cloud over the title of the plaintiff and it will not be necessary for the plaintiff to sue for declaration and a suit for injunction may be sufficient.

Where the plaintiff, believing that defendant is only a trespasser or a wrongful claimant without title, files a mere suit for injunction, and in such a suit, the defendant discloses in his defence the details of the right or title claimed by him, which raises a serious dispute or cloud over O.S. No.26291/2020 plaintiff's title, then there is a need for the plaintiff, to amend the plaint and convert the suit into one for declaration.
Alternatively, he may withdraw the suit for bare injunction, with permission of the court to file a comprehensive suit for declaration and injunction.
He may file the suit for declaration with consequential relief, even after the suit for injunction is dismissed, where the suit raised only the issue of possession and not any issue of title.
26. Admittedly the suit schedule property is site property.
When it is site property the plaintiff has to establish formation of sites in Sy.No.160 by his vendor, conversion of said property for residential purpose.

That apart after the above stated notifications the award is also passed as per Ex.D4.
O.S. No.26291/2020 27.

He also relied upon Judgment reported in Civil Appeal No.7662/1997 (Rame Gowda (D) by Lrs.,
Vs. M.Varadappa Naidu (D) by Lrs., and another) wherein it is held that:
It is thus clear that so far as the Indian law is concerned the person in peaceful possession is entitled to retain his possession and in order to protect such possession he may even use reasonable force to keep out a trespasser.
A rightful owner who has been wrongfully dispossessed of land may retake possession if he can do so peacefully and without the use of unreasonable force.

If the trespasser is in settled possession of the property belonging to the rightful owner, the rightful owner shall have to take recourse to law; he cannot take the law in his own hands and evict the trespasser or interfere with his possession.

The law will come to the aid of a person in peaceful and settled possession by injuncting even a rightful owner from using force or taking law in his own hands, and also by restoring him in possession even from the rightful owner (of course subject to the law of limitation), if the latter has dispossessed the prior possessor by use of force.
In the absence of proof of better title, possession or prior peaceful settled possession is itself evidence of title.

Law presumes the O.S.
No.26291/2020 possession to go with the title unless rebutted.

The owner of any property may prevent even by using reasonable force a trespasser from an attempted trespass, when it is in the process of being committed, or is of a flimsy character, or recurring, intermittent, stray or casual in nature, or has just been committed, while the rightful owner did not have enough time to have recourse to law.
In the last of he cases, the possession of the trespasser, just entered into would not be called as one acquiesced to by the true owner.

sentences.text: The second aspect is this.
It is part of the concept of "Rule of Law" that no claim to a right to dispossess by the use of force without recourse to procedure in accordance with law is recognised or countenanced by Courts.
Such a right in the respondent cannot be recognised regardless of the question whether or not the appellant itself has any subsisting right to remain in possession.

The protection that the Court affords is not of the possession - which in the circumstances is litigious possession and cannot be equated with lawful possession - but a protection against forcible dispossession.
The basis of relief is a corollary of the principle that even with the best of title there can be no forcible dispossession.

It is well settled that weakness of the defendant is not a trump card to decree the suit of plaintiff.

33. At this stage it is necessary to note that in a decision reported in (2013) 3 SCC 66 in case of Commissioner, Bangalore Development Authority and another Vs. Brijesh Reddy and another,
wherein it is held that, "it is clear that the Land Acquisition Act is a complete code in itself and is meant to serve public purpose.

sentences.text: By necessary implication, the power of the civil court to take cognizance of the case under Section 9 CPC stands excluded and a civil court has no jurisdiction to go into the question of the validity or legality of the notification under Sec.4 declaration under section 6 and subsequent O.S. No.26291/2020 proceedings except by the High Court in a proceeding under Article 226 of the Constitution.
It is thus clear that the Civil Court is devoid of jurisdiction to give declaration or even bare injunction....."

No doubt, in the case on hand, the plaintiffs approached the civil court with a prayer only for permanent injunction restraining defendants No.1 and 2 i.e., BDA, their agents, servants and anyone claiming through them from interfering with the peaceful possession and enjoyment of the schedule property.
It is true that there is no challenge to the acquisition proceeding.

However, in view of the assertion of the BDA, in their written statements, about the initiation of acquisition proceedings ending with the passing of award, handing over possession and subsequent action, etc.
said suit is not maintainable.
This was rightly concluded by the trial court.
For proper compensation, the aggrieved parties are free to avail the statutory provisions and approach the court concerned.
All these aspects have been clearly noted by the trial court and ultimately rightly dismissed the suit as not maintainable.

On the other hand, the learned Single Judge of the High Court though adverted to the principles laid down by this court with reference to acquisition of land under Land Acquisition Act and Section 9 of CPC O.S. No.26291/2020 committed an error in Amjad Baig vs The Commissioner, Bda on 2 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20730624/

34. It is also necessary to note that in a recent decision in Civil Appeal No. 2749/2023 in case of Land and Building Department Through Secretary and Another V/s Attro Devi and others the Hon'ble Apex Court was pleased to observe that:
"when the State Government acquires land and drawn up a memorandum of taking possession, that amounts to taking the physical possession of the land on the large chunk of property or otherwise which is acquired

, the Government is not supposed to O.S. No.26291/2020 put some other person or the police force in possession to retain it and start cultivating it till the land is used by it for the purpose for which it has been acquired.
The Government is not supposed to start residing or to physically occupy it once possession has been taken by drawing the inquest proceedings for obtaining possession thereof.

Thereafter, if any further retaining of land or any re-entry is made on the land or someone starts cultivation on the open land or starts residing in the outhouse, etc., is deemed to be the trespasser on land which in possession of the State....."
Thus, it is apparent that vesting is with possession and the statute has provided under section 16 and 17 of the Act of 1894 that once possession is taken, absolute vesting occurred.
It is an indefeasible right and vesting is with possession thereafter.

The vesting specified under Section 16, takes place after various steps, such as, notification under Section 4, declaration under Section 6, notice under Section 9, award under Section 11 and then possession.
The statutory provision of vesting of property absolutely free from all encumbrances has to be accorded full effect.
Not only the possession vests in the State but all other encumbrances are also removed forthwith.
The title of the landholder ceases and the state becomes the absolute owner and in possession of the property.
Thereafter there is no control of the landowner over the property.
He cannot have any animus to take the property and to control it.
Even if he has O.S. No.26291/2020 retained the possession or otherwise trespassed upon it after possession has been taken by the State, he is a trespasser".

37. No doubt it is true, in some of decisions relied by learned counsel for plaintiff it is observed that,
even in case, plaintiff is in possession of suit property illegally, they are entitled for injunction till defendant authority takes proper recourse under law, but as already discussed, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Brijesh Reddy case has clearly held, even suit for injunction is not maintainable once acquisition proceedings were concluded.

Taking into note of principles laid down in above decision,
plaintiff cannot claim injunctive relief against defendant authority by contending, they themselves and their vendor has been continued in settled possession of suit property.
Hence, the document produced by the plaintiff are totally insufficient to hold that the plaintiff is in possession of suit schedule property as on the date of O.S. No.26291/2020 filing of this suit.

Except the sale deed,
GPA, khatha certificate and register extract of house and vacant sites, the plaintiff has not produced any other document to show where exactly the suit schedule property is situated in Sy.No.160 and so also his lawful possession over the suit schedule property as on the date of suit.

Without establishing the basic requirements of the suit for bare injunction the assertion of the plaintiff that he is in lawful possession over the suit schedule property as on the date of filing of suit has no weight.
The plaintiff though asserted that he constructed structure in the suit schedule property no such document to establish the construction of structure is produced before the court.
Copy of sanction plan or license is not produced.

Therefore the assertion of the plaintiff that he is in lawful possession of suit property and constructed structure therein having acquired the same under the Registered Sale Deed appears to be unreasonable to accept.
Accordingly, I answered Issue No.1 in the negative.
38. Issue No.2:
The plaintiff so as to prove this issue has mainly relied upon the oral evidence of PW.1.
However the alleged interference is categorically denied by the defendant in his written statement.
No evidence as such is placed to prove that the officials of defendant tried to interfere with the possession of the suit schedule property.
Plaintiff has miserably failed to prove his lawful possession or settled possession as on the date of suit with cogent and convincing evidence.
Though he claims that he acquired title in respect of suit property by sale deed, but the flow of title has not been established.
Therefore the case of the plaintiff that he acquired the possession of suit schedule property under the sale deed is unreasonable to accept.
When the plaintiff failed to prove his lawful possession over the suit property as on the date of suit question of considering the alleged interference not O.S. No.26291/2020 arises.
Even otherwise as stated above the plaintiff failed to produce any evidence to show the alleged interference by the defendant.
Accordingly, I answered Issue No.2 in the negative.
39. Issue No.3:-
In the case on hand absolutely plaintiff has not placed any evidence to show that as on the date of execution of sale deed as per Ex.P.4 his vendor was having title over suit property.
The plaintiff failed to prove flow of title to his vendor in respect of suit property.

As could be seen from the documents as on the date of execution of sale deed in favour of the plaintiff or as on the date of Amjad Baig vs The Commissioner, Bda on 2 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20730624/

It is not case of plaintiff that, there was De-notification of acquired land by the government of by court order and land again vest with original owner.

Under these circumstance, it can safely inferred that, though suit property was acquired by BDA in the year 1978 itself O.S. No.26291/2020 and possession of property has already taken by BDA, plaintiff has created sale deed as per Ex.P.4 and GPA as per Ex.P6.
Merely because plaintiff has put up illegal construction over suit property, he is not entitled of injunctive relief as prayed in suit.
The defendant authority which acquired suit property and passed award become absolute owner of the same.
Now plaintiff who has continued as trespasser in suit property cannot seek injunction against defendant who is lawful owner of suit property from exercising its right over suit property.
As such, plaintiff is not entitled for any relief as prayed in plaint.

Judgment
A rightful owner who has been wrongfully dispossessed of land may retake possession if he can do so peacefully and without the use of unreasonable force.
If the trespasser is in settled possession of the property belonging to the rightful owner, the rightful owner shall have to take recourse to law; he cannot take the law in his own hands and evict the trespasser or interfere with his possession.
The law will come to the aid of a person in peaceful and settled possession by injuncting even a rightful owner from using force or taking law in his own hands, and also by restoring him in possession even from the rightful owner (of course subject to the law of limitation), if the latter has dispossessed the prior possessor by use of force.
In the absence of proof of better title, possession or prior peaceful settled possession is itself evidence of title.
Law presumes the O.S.
No.26291/2020 possession to go with the title unless rebutted.
The owner of any property may prevent even by using reasonable force a trespasser from an attempted trespass, when it is in the process of being committed, or is of a flimsy character, or recurring, intermittent, stray or casual in nature, or has just been committed, while the rightful owner did not have enough time to have recourse to law.
In the last of he cases, the possession of the trespasser, just entered into would not be called as one acquiesced to by the true owner.
The High Court has also not gone into that question.
But the High Court has dismissed the plaintiff's suit on the sole ground that the plaintiff has not satisfactorily proved his title.
O.S. No.26291/2020

The Corporation of the City of Bangalore)

The second aspect is this.
It is part of the concept of "Rule of Law" that no claim to a right to dispossess by the use of force without recourse to procedure in accordance with law is recognised or countenanced by Courts.
Such a right in the respondent cannot be recognised regardless of the question whether or not the appellant itself has any subsisting right to remain in possession.
The protection that the Court affords is not of the possession - which in the circumstances is litigious possession and cannot be equated with lawful possession - but a protection against forcible dispossession.
The basis of relief is a corollary of the principle that even with the best of title there can be no forcible dispossession.
